Paper_name: Sticking together? Re-binding previous other-associated stimuli interferes with self-verification but not partner-verification
Summary: The study investigates whether the 'we-prioritisation' effect extends to individual task partners, similar to the self-prioritisation effect where self-relevant stimuli are processed faster. Pairs of participants performed a joint shape-label matching task where identities (self, partner, stranger) were assigned to shapes and then switched halfway. Results showed a standard self-prioritisation effect with faster responses to self-stimuli. After remapping, performance decreased for self-trials but improved for partner- and stranger-stimuli. No evidence was found for an enhanced representation for task-partner identities, but interference between old and new memory traces affected self-retrieval processes.
Author: Merryn D. Constable, Günther Knoblich
Conclusion: The experiment found no evidence for partner-prioritisation, as task-partner-associated identities did not benefit from an enhanced memory representation. However, switching identity associations caused interference specifically for self-verification processes, slowing responses to newly mapped self-stimuli. This suggests that while self-prioritisation is robust, the binding and re-binding of identity-relevant information in memory can disrupt self-retrieval when previous associations conflict.
